p2: A strange transaction reaches a Binance wallet.
The vault that has to stay open, online, so every customer can withdraw their money at any moment.
The hacker's problem: every order sent from this wallet carries a number.
No way to know which number will be the right one.
More than one point six billion dollars in Tether.
No one at Binance authorized it.
p3: About one hundred forty-four billion dollars in assets, according to DefiLlama.
Its founder, CZ, no longer runs it.
But he is still its majority shareholder.
This fortress has been hit before.
May 2019: seven thousand bitcoins vanish from a hot wallet.
CZ considers rolling back the Bitcoin blockchain.
He had already created an emergency fund: SAFU.
And a misspelled phrase that became a legend: "Funds are SAFU."
Seven years later: about one hundred fifty times more money.
p4: 8:32 p.m.: an on-chain researcher raises the alarm.
The hacker's address was funded through Tornado Cash.
A service built to erase tracks.
9:15 p.m.: CZ posts on X: "This does look like a Binance hack."
Its official statement is edited twice in thirteen minutes.
In the shadows, hundreds of employees fight to take back control.
Around two a.m. Paris time, Binance regains control of Binance 14.
p5: Within the hour, Tether freezes nearly a billion dollars in USDT.
Then more than one and a half billion.
Circle blocks about eight hundred twenty-three million USDC.
The hacker doesn't stop: he deposits sixty million USDT on Aave to borrow forty-four million dollars in ETH.
Around 10:15 p.m., Binance shuts everything down.
After midnight, co-founder Yi He promises: Binance will cover all losses.
Then, on Friday, CZ writes that a pregnant employee worked through the night, alongside hundreds of others.
And: "It hurts, but we will survive."
The toll: about three billion frozen.
p6: More than six hundred million dollars in leveraged bets are liquidated in one hour.
Bitcoin falls to its lowest level in six weeks.
A Standard Chartered analyst warns: the drop could continue as long as the uncertainty lasts.
p7: Binance points to an almost mundane detail: a DevOps engineer's laptop.
No one knows his name, or how.
That computer reportedly opened access to a service container.
And from there, unauthorized withdrawals were submitted.
Binance found no evidence of a private key leak.
So who signed the fifty authorizations?
The orders reportedly went through Binance's own pipeline.
You open your computer, like a thousand times before.
And somewhere, someone was waiting for that move.
p8: One and a half billion dollars.
There too, it all started with a developer's computer.
A fake project, disguised as an investment simulator, according to Safe's investigation.
Back then, CZ asked: how did they hack that machine?
Today, it's Binance's turn to answer.
Richard Teng already pushes back: this was not a "one-click" attack.
Other breach points have been found.
p9: Go back to the lit window.
TRM Labs points to TraderTraitor, North Korea's elite hacking unit.
Then the FBI confirms: it's them.
ZachXBT finds, at the same address, Binance's money and the proceeds of a Bitget hack in September.
In 2022, South Korean intelligence estimated these hackers had stolen one point one billion over five years.
That night, in twenty minutes: nearly six times more.
p10: It says it has covered ninety-five percent of the losses.
